opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for us it really came down to accessibility. When you release a model like Chai-1, you can put the weights and the code out there, but the reality is that a huge fraction of the people who would actually benefit from it — bench scientists, wet-lab biologists, folks at smaller biotechs or academic labs — aren't going to spin up a GPU, wrangle dependencies, and set up MSA pipelines just to try it out. That's a real barrier.

So we wanted day one to be the day anyone could paste in a sequence, maybe add a ligand or some restraints, hit a button, and get a structure back. That matters a lot for getting honest feedback, too. If only ML people can run your model, you only hear from ML people. Putting it in a browser means you start hearing from the people who actually design molecules for a living — where it works, where it breaks, what features they wish it had.

And honestly, part of it was just showing what the model could do. Benchmarks are one thing, but letting people poke at it on their own targets is a much more convincing demonstration. It was a scramble to get the infrastructure ready alongside the release, but I think it was the right call. Releasing the model without an easy way to use it would have felt like only doing half the job.

r001.rationale: The response says many intended users would face a real barrier to using the released weights and code because they would need to set up GPUs, dependencies, and MSA pipelines. It explains the web server made access easier and encouraged those users to try the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to who we wanted to reach. The whole point of releasing Chai-1 was to get it into the hands of people doing real drug discovery work, and a lot of those people are wet-lab biologists or medicinal chemists. They're not going to clone a repo, set up a CUDA environment, and debug dependency conflicts just to try a structure prediction. If the only entry point is a GitHub README, you've effectively filtered your users down to ML engineers, which is a tiny slice of the people who'd actually benefit.

So we felt like the weights and the code alone weren't really a release. A release is something a scientist can use on day one. The web server lets someone paste in a sequence, maybe a ligand SMILES, hit run, and get a structure back in a few minutes with no setup. That felt like the difference between "we published a model" and "we shipped a tool."

The timing part was also deliberate. There's a window right after a release where people are curious and willing to try something. If the server shows up three months later, most of that attention is gone. We wanted the paper, the code, and the server to land together so that whoever heard about it could immediately go kick the tires, whatever their technical background.

And frankly, it was useful for us too. Running it as a service meant we saw what people actually submitted, including the weird edge cases we hadn't thought about, like strange modified residues or very large complexes. That feedback loop was way faster than waiting for GitHub issues to trickle in.

r001.rationale: The response says wet-lab biologists and medicinal chemists would find cloning a repo and setting up the environment cumbersome, and that the web server lets them try the model without setup.

astra-6.text: We wanted to make it easy for people to actually try the model. Releasing the code and weights is useful, but there’s still a barrier if you have to set up an environment and get access to a GPU. A web server lets someone come in with a sequence and run a prediction without doing all of that. So it was a way to get Chai 1 into more people’s hands quickly and start learning from how they use it.

r001.rationale: The response says that releasing the code and weights still leaves users to set up an environment and get GPU access, and that the web server lowers this barrier and gets the model into more people’s hands.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to make it easy for people to actually try the model. Releasing the code and the weights is great, but there’s still a barrier if you have to set up an environment and get access to a GPU before you can run a prediction. A web server lets someone come in with a sequence and a question and just see what happens. We also wanted to learn from that—what people were trying to do, where they got stuck, and what we needed to improve.

r001.rationale: The response says the web server makes the model easier to try by avoiding environment setup and GPU access, but it does not mention or clearly communicate that accessing the model through a Git repository is cumbersome.
